# Question 1

## For the Setup 

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d

data("ny_noaa")

```


## Data Description 

```{r}

ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.)))) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "prop_missing") |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)
range(ny_noaa$date)

```
The dataset has `r format(nrow(ny_noaa), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns, with daily weather observations from ``r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)`` New York stations between 1981 and 2010 . Key variables include id (station), date, prcp (precipitation in tenths of mm), snow (snowfall in mm), snwd (snow depth in mm), and tmax/tmin (tenths of °C). Missingness is large, especially for tmax and tmin (found to be 44% each), snwd (23%), and snow (15%), while prcp is missing less often (6%). There are many stations that didn't record all variables, due to this the summaries need na.rm = TRUE. 

## Cleaning

```{r}

noaa_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10)

noaa_df |> 
  count(snow, name = "n_obs") |> 
  arrange(desc(n_obs))

```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0, because most days in New York have no snowfall. NA is the second most common (381,221 observations), as a lot of stations don't even record the snowfall. Among nonzero values, the most common are 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm and 76 mm. These correspond to 1, ½, 2, and 3 inches, which is indicitave of the fact that snowfall was recorded in inches and converted to millimeters.

## Mean tmax by station in January and July 
```{r}
tmax_station_df = 
  noaa_df |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  mutate(month = if_else(month == 1, "January", "July")) |> 
  group_by(id, month, year) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ungroup()

tmax_station_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .3) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature by station, January vs. July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean max temperature (C)",
    caption = "Data from the NY NOAA dataset"
  )

tmax_station_df |> 
  group_by(month) |> 
  filter(min_rank(mean_tmax) < 4)
```
The average max temperatures in January range from around (-13°C to 10°C), while July averages cluster between arounf 22°C and 32°C. Stations move together from year to year, with warm and cold years showing up across nearly all stations. This points to regional weather, rather than station-specific differences, as the main driver of the pattern. Both year-to-year and station-to-station variation are much greater in January than in July.The lowest values in each month stand out as outliers. In January, station USC00301723 in 1982 has the lowest average (-13.4°C), followed by USC00305925 in 2005 (-12.2°C) and USC00306957 in 2004 (-10.8°C). In July, station USC00308962 in 1988 has an average of 14.0°C, far below the typical range, and USC00302454 in 2004 (18.3°C) and USC00308946 in 1984 (19.1°C) are also unusually low.

## tmax vs tmin - snowfall by year 
```{r}
ggp_temp = 
  noaa_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  scale_fill_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 30000, 50000)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Daily tmax vs. tmin",
    x = "Minimum daily temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum daily temperature (C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) + 
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm"))
ggp_snow = 
  noaa_df |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) + 
  scale_y_discrete(breaks = seq(1985, 2010, 5)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

ggp_temp + ggp_snow

```
The hex plot shows the density and this plot shows us that tmax and tmin are positively related.Most observations are concentrated in a single band roughly 10 to 25°C for both. The yearly snowfall distributions look very similar to one another. All are right-skewed. A few outliers appear, such as tmax near 60°C and some days with tmin above tmax. 

# Question 2

```{r}

covar_df = 
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = 
      case_match(
        sex, 
        1 ~ "male", 
        2 ~ "female"),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    education = 
      case_match(
        education, 
        1 ~ "Less than high school", 
        2 ~ "High school equivalent", 
        3 ~ "More than high school"),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")))

accel_df = 
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df = 
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")

```

```{r}

nhanes_summary = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  summarize(
    n_participants = n(),
    n_male = sum(sex == "male"),
    n_female = sum(sex == "female"))

```

The final dataset includes `r nhanes_df |> nrow()` participants aged 21 or older with complete demographic data (`r nhanes_df |> filter(sex == "male") |> nrow()` male and `r nhanes_df |> filter(sex == "female") |> nrow()` female), out of the 250 originally observed. It contains all original variables: participant ID (seqn), sex, age, BMI, education, and the MIMS values for each of the 1,440 minutes of the day (min1 to min1440). Sex and education are factors, ordered by education level for tables and plots.

## Visualization of the age distributions 
```{r}

nhanes_df |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable()

```
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6) + 
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by education level and sex",
    x = "Education level",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex",
    caption = "Data from NHANES"
  )
```
The sample is relatively balanced between men and women in the less than high school (27 men, 28 women) and more than high school (56 men, 59 women) groups, while the high school equivalent group has more men than women which is slightly different than the other groups  (35 vs. 23). Most participants have more than high school education. Median age is similar for men and women in the less than high school group (about 60), and participants with more than high school education are younger (median is among the low 40s). In the high school equivalent group, women are older than men (median about 60 for women whereas the median for men lies in the 50s range).

## Total activity variable for each participant
```{r}

total_df = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims") |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims)) |> 
  ungroup()

total_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .5) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily MIMS",
    color = "Sex",
    caption = "Data from NHANES"
  )

```
Total activity is seen to decline with age in all three groups, but the shape is a bit different from each other. In the less than high school group, activity falls steadily and men and women follow similar curves. In the high school equivalent group, women are more active than men until about age 55, and then both drop and overlap by a bit. In the more than high school group, activity is relativly flat until about age 60 and then declines more. Women are more active than men across most of the age range and then the two groups end up  converge by age 80. Individual values vary widely at every age, so the trendline/smooth describe averages only. One man in the more than high school group, around age 40 years of age, has a total close to zero making this person a heavy outlier and could also potentially mean the device was not worn properly. 


```{r}

nhanes_long_df = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims") |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes_long_df |> 
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |> 
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .4) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  scale_x_continuous(
  breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080),
  labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM")) + 
 labs(
  title = "24-hour activity time course by education level and sex",
  x = "Time of day",
  y = "Mean MIMS",
  color = "Sex",
  caption = "Data from NHANES"
)+
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```
As we can see, in all the groups, activity is lowest in the early morning and then proceeds to rise, stays high through the middle of the day, and declines through the evening. there is a difference that can be noticed in the patter with the addition of Education level and sex change. In the less than high school group, activity peaks later morning and falls steadily afterward. Men and women are similar during the day, but men are more active overnight and at the end of the day. In the high school equivalent group, women are more active than men from the morning rise until mid-afternoon, and the two groups converge in the evening. In the more than high school group, the sex gap is largest and lasts longer as well. In the two higher education groups, women activity also start to rise earlier in the morning than men. The less than high school group declines earliest in comparison.

# Question 3 

```{r}

jan_2020_df = 
  read_csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan", year = 2020)

july_2020_df = 
  read_csv("./data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "July", year = 2020)

jan_2024_df = 
  read_csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan", year = 2024)

july_2024_df = 
  read_csv("./data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "July", year = 2024)

citibike_df = 
  bind_rows(jan_2020_df, july_2020_df, jan_2024_df, july_2024_df) |> 
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("Jan", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays, 
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type, levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike")),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual, levels = c("member", "casual"))) |> 
  select(ride_id, year, month, weekdays, everything())

citibike_df

citibike_df |> 
  summarize(
    mean_duration = mean(duration),
    median_duration = median(duration),
    max_duration = max(duration))


```
The cleaned dataset has `r citibike_df |> summarize(n = n()) |> pull(n)` rides drawn from four samples: January and July of 2020 and 2024. Each row is one ride. Variables are the ride ID, the year and month of the sample, the day of the week (weekdays), the bike type (rideable_type: classic or electric), the ride duration in minutes (duration), the start and end station names, and rider type (member_casual). 43 rides are missing a start station name and 207 are missing an end station name, and no other variable has missing values. There is a median of about `r citibike_df |> summarize(m = round(median(duration), 1)) |> pull(m)` minutes and a maximum of about `r citibike_df |> summarize(m = round(max(duration))) |> pull(m)` minutes. 

## Rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members

```{r}

citibike_df |> 
  count(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable()

```
Members take a lot more rides than casual riders in every month observed. However, there is a much larger share in July among casual riders as compared to Jan. The number of rides is higher in summer than in winter for both groups, and the difference is larger for casual riders. Rides also grew over the years between 2020 and 2024.


## The 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024

```{r}
citibike_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |> 
  count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides") |> 
  filter(min_rank(desc(n_rides)) < 6) |> 
  arrange(desc(n_rides)) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

The top five are close together, from 146 to 163 sampled rides.

## Plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration.
```{r}

citibike_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")) + 
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by day of the week, month, and year",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year",
    caption = "Data from Citi Bike"
  )
```
July rides are longer than January rides in both years, and 2020 rides are longer than 2024 rides in when comparing the same month. In 2020, weekend rides are longer than weekday rides. In July 2024, weekend rides are also longer whereas in January 2024 there is no clear weekend pattern, since Saturday is the highest day and Sunday is the lowest. Overall, the weekend effect is largest in summer, and the gap between 2020 and 2024 is larger than the gap between any two days of the week.

## Impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration
```{r}

citibike_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans = "sqrt",
    breaks = c(0, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration by month, membership status, and bike type, 2024",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes in the square-root scale)",
    fill = "Bike type",
    caption = "Data from Citi Bike"
  )

```
As seen on the graph, membership status has the largest effect on ride duration. Casual riders based on the median seen take longer rides than members in every month and on both bike types. Bike type matters differently by membership. Among casual riders, classic bikes are used for longer rides than electric bikes. Among the members, the two bike types are closer to each other and doesn't show too much of a difference, with electric bikes slightly longer in July  and very similar in January . Month also matters as we can see that July rides are longer than January rides  for casual riders on both bike types and for members on electric bikes, while member rides on classic bikes change little.
